objects.visualHint: Look for a bright round glow with a grainy outer edge and a dense center.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M3 is a globular cluster, a dense sphere of ancient stars orbiting the Milky Way. The bright center is crowded with stars too close together to fully separate in the image.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Globular clusters preserve some of the oldest stars in the galaxy. They are deep-time objects, carrying clues from the Milky Way's early history.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: These clusters were once listed as fuzzy objects by early observers, but telescopes revealed them as swarms of stars. They are among the most satisfying objects to watch sharpen during live stacking.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for a round glow that becomes grainy. The outer edges may resolve into star points while the center stays bright and crowded.

objects.description: A bright, moderately concentrated ball of ancient stars near the center of Ophiuchus.
wowFacts: M10 is an ancient globular cluster drifting through the halo of the Milky Way.
Its stars formed long before the Sun and planets existed.
The cluster is a gravitational swarm, with stars packed far closer than in our neighborhood.
In the live image, M10 should grow from a soft ball into a grainy cluster.
objects.visualHint: Look for a round, moderately bright glow with stars resolving around the edges.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M10 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is a dense, old collection of stars bound together by gravity.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Globular clusters like M10 preserve ancient stellar populations. They help astronomers trace the history and structure of the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Ophiuchus is the serpent-bearer, a large constellation crossed by the summer sky. It contains several globular clusters, making it a rewarding region for deep-sky observing.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: M10 is not as famous as M13, but it is a satisfying cluster. Look for a bright center and a softer outer halo that becomes textured with time.

objects.description: A looser, more relaxed globular cluster than most of its neighbors, sitting a few degrees from M10.
wowFacts: M12 is a globular cluster that appears looser than many of its ancient relatives.
It may have lost some of its lower-mass stars through gravitational interactions with the Milky Way.
The stars here are relics from the galaxy's early history.
In the live image, M12 may look softer and less centrally packed than classic globulars.
objects.visualHint: Look for a round, slightly loose cluster with a gentle brightening toward the center.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M12 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is a gravitationally bound swarm of old stars.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M12 is interesting because it is relatively loose for a globular cluster. Its structure may tell a story of stars stripped away over time.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M12 sits near M10 in the same broad summer region. Together they show that even objects of the same class can have different personalities.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a modest, grainy glow rather than a dramatic compact ball. Compare it with denser globular clusters if both are shown.

objects.description: A large, distant globular cluster, fainter than its more famous neighbors but rich in ancient stars.
objects.sizeDescription: about a third of the full Moon
wowFacts: M14 is a distant globular cluster whose stars blur together into a soft ancient glow.
It contains a large population of old stars orbiting the Milky Way.
A nova was later found in M14 on old photographic plates, showing that even ancient clusters can host sudden stellar events.
In the live image, M14 may stay smoother than closer, brighter globulars.
objects.visualHint: Look for a faint round glow with only limited resolution into individual stars.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M14 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is farther and harder to resolve than some of the brighter summer globulars.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Clusters like M14 contain ancient stars and occasional stellar surprises such as novae. They are not frozen relics; their stars can still change and erupt.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M14 is one of several globular clusters cataloged by Messier in Ophiuchus. It is a quieter target, best appreciated as part of the galaxy's old halo population.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This may appear as a soft circular haze more than a resolved star swarm. Dark skies and steady tracking help bring out its shape.

objects.description: One of the densest globular clusters known, a tightly packed swarm of several hundred thousand stars.
objects.sizeDescription: about a quarter of the full Moon
wowFacts: M80 is a compact globular cluster with a very dense-looking core.
Its ancient stars are packed into a tight sphere far from the Sun.
A nova appeared in M80 in 1860, briefly changing the cluster's appearance.
In the live image, M80 is small but intense, with a bright center.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small, concentrated glow with a bright core and subtle grain around it.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M80 is a globular cluster in Scorpius. It is compact and dense compared with many easier, looser clusters.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Dense clusters are laboratories for stellar encounters. In crowded environments, stars can interact in ways that are rare in quieter parts of the galaxy.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M80 lies in the dramatic constellation Scorpius, low in the summer south from Greece. Its 19th-century nova made it especially notable among globular clusters.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Because it is compact, M80 may look almost star-like at first. Watch for the surrounding glow that distinguishes it from a single star.

objects.description: A loose, faint globular cluster, one of the last Messier objects to be discovered.
objects.sizeDescription: about a third of the full Moon
wowFacts: M107 is one of the fainter globular clusters in the Messier catalog.
Its ancient stars form a loose, subtle swarm in Ophiuchus.
This cluster is less showy, but it carries the same deep-time history as brighter globulars.
In a live image, the reward is seeing a faint old cluster gradually separate from the background.
objects.visualHint: Look for a faint, loose, roundish glow that may only partly resolve into stars.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M107 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is a relatively faint, loose cluster of old stars.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Not every ancient cluster is bright and dramatic. M107 shows the quieter end of the globular cluster family.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M107 was added to the Messier catalog after Messier's original publications. It is a patient observer's target rather than an instant showpiece.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This object may be subtle, especially with light pollution or low altitude. Look for a slight concentration of faint stars and haze.

objects.description: A large, loosely concentrated globular cluster, easy to resolve into individual stars even in modest telescopes.
objects.sizeDescription: about two-thirds of the full Moon
wowFacts: M55 is a large, loose globular cluster in Sagittarius.
Its stars are ancient, but the cluster appears more open than many dense globulars.
From dark skies, it can spread into a broad grainy glow.
In the live image, M55 may look like a gentle cloud of old stars rather than a tight ball.
objects.visualHint: Look for a broad, loose, grainy glow with no extremely sharp central core.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M55 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a large, relatively loose swarm of old stars.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M55 shows that globular clusters vary widely in concentration. Its looser structure makes it visually different from dense clusters like M15.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Sagittarius contains many treasures because it points toward the Milky Way's rich inner regions. M55 is one of its broad, understated globular clusters.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This target benefits from dark skies and a clear southern horizon. Look for a wide soft patch that becomes grainier with stacking.

objects.description: A rich, loose scattering of over a hundred stars in the rich starfields of Sagittarius.
wowFacts: M23 is a loose open cluster set in one of the richest star fields of the summer Milky Way.
Its stars were born together and are slowly drifting apart into the galaxy.
This cluster sits near the direction of the Milky Way's crowded inner regions.
In the live image, the beauty is not one bright core but a graceful gathering of individual suns.
objects.visualHint: Look for a loose sprinkling of stars, richer than the surrounding field but not tightly packed.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M23 is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is a group of stars born from the same cloud and still traveling through the Milky Way as a loose family.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters show how stars begin life together before the galaxy gradually scatters them. M23 is a gentle example set against one of the sky's richest backgrounds.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Its location in Sagittarius places it near many famous summer objects. It is less dramatic than the Lagoon or Trifid, but it belongs to the same Milky Way landscape.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for a slightly denser star field rather than a compact glow. The cluster may blend into the background, so compare the richer area with the surrounding stars.

objects.description: A bright, loose cluster of stars easily swept up with binoculars against the dense Sagittarius Milky Way.
wowFacts: M25 is a bright open cluster in Sagittarius, easy to enjoy as a relaxed star pattern.
Its stars are young compared with the Sun and still share a common birthplace.
Some stars in this cluster vary in brightness, adding hidden change to what looks like a still scene.
In the live image, M25 should appear as a broad, loose gathering rather than a dense knot.
objects.visualHint: Look for a broad, loose group of bright stars against the summer Milky Way.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M25 is an open cluster in Sagittarius. Its stars formed together and remain loosely associated as they orbit within the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters help astronomers compare stars that formed at about the same time. They are natural laboratories for understanding how stars age at different masses.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M25 is one of several Messier objects packed into the Sagittarius region. It is a calmer stop on a summer tour dominated by nebulae and dense star clouds.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a star cluster, not nebulosity. The brighter stars define the view first, while fainter members fill in as the image settles.

objects.description: A compact, tightly packed knot of young hot stars near the Trifid Nebula.
objects.sizeDescription: about a third of the full Moon
wowFacts: M21 is a young open cluster sitting close to the Trifid Nebula in the summer sky.
Its hot young stars formed recently by cosmic standards.
The cluster sits in a neighborhood where star clusters and glowing clouds appear side by side.
In the live image, M21 is a crisp star group beside some of the Milky Way's great nebular scenery.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact group of bright young stars, often near richer nebulous fields.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M21 is an open cluster in Sagittarius near the Trifid Nebula. It contains young stars born from the Milky Way's gas and dust.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M21 helps show the connection between star clusters and star-forming regions. Clusters like this are what can remain after a nebula has formed stars and begun to disperse.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M21 is often visited together with M20 and M8 during summer observing. It is part of a region that feels like a guided tour through star birth.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for individual stars rather than a cloud. The cluster is modest, so its setting near brighter nebulae is part of the appeal.

objects.description: A small, modest cluster of stars, easy to pass by between the more famous nebulae of Sagittarius.
objects.sizeDescription: a quarter of the full Moon
wowFacts: M18 is a small young star family tucked between brighter summer showpieces.
Its stars are much younger than the Sun and were born together in the Milky Way.
This cluster sits between the Omega Nebula and the rich Sagittarius region, like a quiet waypoint on the Milky Way road.
In the live image, M18 is a modest pattern of stars rather than a dramatic glow.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small, loose cluster of stars against a rich background field.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M18 is an open cluster in Sagittarius. It is a modest group of young stars born together from the same star-forming environment.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Even small clusters are part of the Milky Way's star-making story. They show that star birth often produces groups, not isolated stars.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M18 sits in a region full of famous summer objects, including the Omega and Lagoon nebulae. It is a quieter member of the same rich sky route.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Do not expect a dense cluster or nebula. Look for a small grouping that stands out slightly from the surrounding Milky Way field.

objects.description: A modest but distinct cluster of stars, sitting in a rich stretch of the Scutum Milky Way.
wowFacts: M26 is a compact open cluster in Scutum, near the dense star fields of the summer Milky Way.
Dust between us and the cluster may dim part of its star field.
Its stars formed together and are slowly being pulled apart by the galaxy.
In the live image, M26 may appear as a small, understated knot of stars.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact, faint cluster of stars with a slightly uneven appearance.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M26 is an open cluster in Scutum. It is a group of stars born together in the Milky Way's disk.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters help astronomers compare stars of common age and origin. M26 also hints at how foreground dust can hide or dim parts of the galaxy.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Scutum is a small constellation near the rich summer Milky Way. M26 is less famous than nearby M11, but it belongs to the same stellar region.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This is a subtle cluster. Look for a small concentration of faint stars rather than a bright showpiece.

objects.description: A rich, young cluster of stars near the Bubble Nebula, easy to sweep up along the rich northern Milky Way.
wowFacts: M52 is a rich open cluster in Cassiopeia, set along the starry path of the Milky Way.
Its stars are young compared with the Sun and still gathered in a recognizable family.
The cluster lies in a region crowded with other clusters, nebulae, and dust clouds.
In the live image, M52 should look like a dense sprinkle of stars with a few brighter anchors.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact cluster with many faint stars and a few brighter anchors.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M52 is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. It contains many stars that formed together and remain gravitationally associated.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters are snapshots of stellar families at different ages. M52 helps show how young clusters populate the Milky Way's disk.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Cassiopeia's W shape is one of the easiest northern patterns to recognize and is tied to Greek mythology. M52 adds a rich telescopic layer to that familiar constellation.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for a tight patch of stars against a busy background. The cluster's richness becomes clearer as fainter stars appear.

objects.description: A compact, triangular knot of stars, one of the last objects Charles Messier ever catalogued.
objects.sizeDescription: a fifth of the full Moon
wowFacts: M103 is a small open cluster in Cassiopeia with a compact triangular look.
Its stars are young members of the Milky Way's disk.
A reddish star in the field can add a warm contrast to the cluster view.
In the live image, M103 is a small pattern target rather than a large showpiece.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact triangular group of stars with a few brighter points.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M103 is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. It is a small group of stars born together in the plane of the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Clusters like M103 help astronomers understand how young stars evolve after birth. Their shared age makes them useful natural laboratories.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M103 was one of the last objects added to Messier's original catalog. It sits in a constellation rich with clusters because Cassiopeia lies along the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This target is small. Look for the shape made by the brighter stars rather than expecting a dense or nebulous object.

objects.description: A bright, loose cluster of young stars, a rewarding binocular target near the Cassiopeia showpieces.
wowFacts: NGC 663 is a rich open cluster in Cassiopeia, one of that constellation's strong star-cluster targets.
It contains many young, hot stars born in the Milky Way's disk.
The cluster sits in a region crowded with other clusters and dark dust.
In the live image, its appeal is the dense star field rather than one bright core.
objects.visualHint: Look for a rich concentration of stars with an uneven, natural scattering.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: NGC 663 is an open cluster in Cassiopeia. It is a young star group embedded in one of the Milky Way's rich northern regions.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: This cluster helps trace recent star formation in our galaxy. Young clusters like it mark places where the Milky Way has recently made new stars.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Cassiopeia is tied to Greek mythology as the vain queen, but through a telescope it is also a treasury of star clusters. NGC 663 is one of its richer examples.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect many individual stars rather than a smooth glow. The cluster may blend with the rich background, so look for the densest concentration.

objects.description: A loose, bright cluster of stars easily seen with the naked eye between Perseus and Andromeda.
objects.sizeDescription: a little more than the full Moon
wowFacts: M34 is a nearby open cluster, a loose family of stars in Perseus.
Its stars are young compared with the Sun but old enough to have spread out noticeably.
The cluster is close enough that several of its stars appear bright and widely spaced.
In the live image, M34 feels like a clean, open gathering of suns.
objects.visualHint: Look for a loose cluster of bright stars spread across the field, not a compact ball.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M34 is an open cluster in Perseus. It contains stars born together that are now loosely spread across space.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters like M34 show how star families gradually disperse. Their stars share an origin, making them useful for studying stellar aging.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Perseus is part of a great Greek mythological sky story involving Andromeda and Cassiopeia. M34 adds a bright telescopic object to that ancient constellation.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This is a star pattern target. Look for a loose, balanced scattering of bright points rather than a fuzzy nebula.

objects.description: A spiral galaxy with a dark dust lane across its bright core, giving it the famous black-eye look.
objects.sizeDescription: about one-third of the full Moon
wowFacts: The Black Eye Galaxy gets its nickname from a dark lane of dust crossing the bright face of the galaxy.
Its inner and outer gas appear to rotate in opposite directions, a clue to a past galactic encounter or merger.
The light in tonight's view has traveled for roughly 17 million years.
In the live image, the prize is the contrast: a bright core with a subtle dark bruise beside it.
objects.visualHint: Look for a bright oval core; the dark dust feature is subtle and needs a good stack and dark sky.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M64 is a spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices. Its famous dark patch is dust inside the galaxy blocking some of the starlight behind it.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: The galaxy's unusual gas motion suggests its history was not quiet. It may have absorbed or interacted with another system, leaving the galaxy with layers that do not all move the same way.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Nicknames like Black Eye help guests recognize real structure rather than just seeing another faint smudge. This is one of the best spring galaxies for that kind of visual storytelling.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: The central glow should appear first. The dark feature is not a bold black stripe in a live stack; look for an uneven edge or shadow near the bright center.

objects.description: A distant ancient globular cluster in Coma Berenices, seen as a compact grainy glow.
objects.sizeDescription: about one-third of the full Moon
wowFacts: M53 is much farther away than many showpiece globular clusters, so its ancient stars blur into a compact glow.
Its stars belong to one of the Milky Way's old halo populations.
From Earth, this dense swarm sits near the soft star fields of Coma Berenices.
In the live image, watch the edge turn grainy as the telescope starts resolving the brightest stars.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small round glow with a brighter center and slight grain around the edge.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M53 is a globular cluster, a dense ball of old stars orbiting far out in the Milky Way's halo. Its distance makes it harder to resolve than brighter summer globulars.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Globular clusters are fossils of the early galaxy. M53 adds a more distant example to the familiar nearby cluster showpieces.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Coma Berenices is named for Berenice's hair, a royal story preserved in the sky. M53 turns that gentle constellation into a deep-time target.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a compact glow rather than a dramatic spray of stars. A longer stack may bring out a grainy outer halo.

objects.description: A large spiral galaxy with an active core and strange extra arms revealed in deeper wavelengths.
objects.sizeDescription: a little over half the full Moon
wowFacts: M106 helped astronomers measure galaxy distances using water-vapor masers orbiting near its central black hole.
It has ordinary spiral arms plus strange extra arms that show up strongly outside visible light.
Its light has traveled for roughly 24 million years to arrive tonight.
In the live image, look for a long soft oval with a bright center rather than crisp spiral arms.
objects.visualHint: Look for an elongated galaxy glow with a stronger core; the outer disk is broad and subtle.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M106 is a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici. It is tilted toward us, so its disk appears as a broad oval rather than a perfect face-on spiral.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M106 is scientifically famous because precise radio observations of water masers near its center helped anchor the cosmic distance scale. It is both beautiful and useful.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: This galaxy was discovered by Pierre Mechain and later became part of the extended Messier catalog. Modern instruments turned it from a faint patch into a measuring tool for the universe.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: The bright core should appear quickly. The larger disk is faint, so judge the view by the growing oval shape rather than expecting obvious arms.

objects.description: A round planetary nebula whose darker internal patches inspired the nickname Owl Nebula.
wowFacts: The Owl Nebula is the glowing outer atmosphere of a dying star, shaped into a faint round shell.
Its owl-like face comes from darker internal regions, not from solid holes in space.
It is only a few thousand light-years away, close enough for telescopes to show its rounded form.
In the live image, the face may be subtle: first look for the pale circular disk.
objects.visualHint: Look for a faint round disk; the owl-eye dark patches are delicate and may need a longer stack.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M97 is a planetary nebula in Ursa Major. A dying star has shed gas into space, and the hot remnant lights that gas from within.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Planetary nebulae show how Sun-like stars return material to the galaxy. The Owl Nebula is a gentle-looking example of a dramatic stellar ending.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: The nickname comes from Lord Rosse's 19th-century drawings, where the darker patches suggested an owl's face. It is a reminder that observers have always used imagination to navigate faint things.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This is a low-surface-brightness object, so it may look ghostly. Let the stack build before hunting for the inner patches.

objects.description: A nearly edge-on spiral galaxy in Ursa Major, appearing as a narrow streak of distant starlight.
objects.sizeDescription: about one-third of the full Moon
wowFacts: M108 is a spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on, so its billions of stars compress into a thin streak.
Its nickname, the Surfboard Galaxy, comes from that long narrow shape.
The light in tonight's view left roughly 46 million years ago.
In the live image, the galaxy may look uneven or mottled rather than smooth.
objects.visualHint: Look for a faint narrow streak with a slightly brighter middle.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M108 is a spiral galaxy in Ursa Major. Because we see it nearly edge-on, the disk appears as a slim line rather than a round spiral.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Edge-on galaxies reveal dust and structure in a different way from face-on spirals. They help guests understand that a galaxy's appearance depends strongly on viewing angle.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M108 sits near the Owl Nebula in the sky, making the pair a nice contrast: one dying star inside our galaxy, one whole galaxy far beyond it.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Do not expect spiral arms. Look for a long, thin glow that slowly separates itself from the background stars.

objects.description: A bright galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, part of the rich galaxy field around Markarian's Chain.
wowFacts: M84 is part of the Virgo Cluster, a city of galaxies rather than a single isolated island.
In this region of sky, several galaxies can crowd into the same telescope neighborhood.
Its light has crossed roughly 60 million years of space before reaching tonight's screen.
In the live image, the magic is context: a small glow that belongs to a much larger galaxy swarm.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact oval glow; nearby faint smudges may be other Virgo Cluster galaxies.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M84 is a bright galaxy in the Virgo Cluster. It appears as a smooth glow rather than a spiral with dramatic arms.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: The Virgo Cluster is the nearest large galaxy cluster to our Local Group. Observing it is like looking toward a crowded downtown of galaxies.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M84 lies in the famous Markarian's Chain region. For observers, this field is a rite of passage because the view can contain multiple galaxies at once.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a small, smooth, pale oval. The field may reward careful looking more than instant drama.

objects.description: A bright Virgo Cluster galaxy often viewed beside M84 in the Markarian's Chain region.
wowFacts: M86 is one member of the Virgo Cluster, where galaxies gather by the thousands.
It sits close to M84 in the sky, turning one telescope view into a small tour of galaxy clustering.
Its light has traveled for roughly 50 million years.
In the live image, look for a quiet oval glow that gains meaning from its galactic neighborhood.
objects.visualHint: Look for a smooth oval glow near other faint galaxy smudges.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M86 is a bright galaxy in Virgo. It is part of the same rich cluster environment as M84 and M87.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Galaxy clusters show that galaxies are not sprinkled randomly through space. Gravity gathers them into enormous families and filaments.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: This is a classic spring galaxy-hopping target. It is less about one famous shape and more about realizing how crowded the deep universe can be.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Look for a soft, round-to-oval glow. If the frame is placed well, more than one galaxy may be visible.

objects.description: A giant galaxy in Virgo whose central black hole became the first black hole ever directly imaged.
objects.sizeDescription: a small bright glow — telescope only
wowFacts: M87 contains the black hole that became humanity's first directly imaged black hole in 2019.
That central black hole has a mass of billions of Suns.
M87 is a giant galaxy near the heart of the Virgo Cluster.
In the live image, the black hole is far too small to see; the glow is the galaxy around it.
objects.visualHint: Look for a smooth bright oval; the famous black hole is not visible, but it sits at the galaxy's core.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M87 is a giant galaxy in Virgo. In a live telescope image it appears as a smooth bright glow, not a spiral or detailed black-hole image.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M87 is one of the great landmarks of modern astronomy because the Event Horizon Telescope imaged the shadow of its central black hole. The guest view shows the host galaxy of that historic target.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: The 2019 black-hole image was made by linking radio telescopes around Earth into a planet-sized instrument. A faint glow in Virgo became a global scientific icon.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a compact smooth glow. The story is larger than the visible detail: you are looking at the galaxy that holds the first black hole ever photographed.

objects.description: A compact globular cluster in Ophiuchus, shining from the dusty direction toward the Milky Way's center.
wowFacts: M9 sits in the rich, dusty direction toward the inner Milky Way.
Its old stars are packed into a compact ball tens of thousands of light-years away.
Dust between us and the cluster dims and reddens some of its light.
In the live image, expect a modest ancient glow rather than a wide resolved swarm.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small compact glow with a brighter middle and only slight grain at the edge.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M9 is a globular cluster in Ophiuchus. It is an old star swarm seen through a busy, dusty part of our galaxy.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Clusters like M9 help trace the Milky Way's halo and inner regions. Even modest globulars are ancient records of galactic history.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Ophiuchus is a rich summer constellation packed with globular clusters. M9 is one stop in that dense deep-sky landscape.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: The cluster may stay compact in the live view. Watch for a small round haze that becomes slightly textured as stacking improves.

objects.description: A compact globular cluster near the Sagittarius star fields and the direction of the Milky Way's center.
wowFacts: M28 lies in Sagittarius, close to the spectacular star fields toward the Milky Way's center.
It is an ancient star swarm, much older than the Sun.
A millisecond pulsar was discovered in M28, showing that dense clusters can host exotic stellar remnants.
In the live image, it should appear as a compact glow with a bright core.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small dense ball of light, with grainy edges if the stack is strong.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M28 is a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is a dense collection of old stars orbiting the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Dense clusters can contain unusual objects such as pulsars, the fast-spinning remains of dead stars. They are old systems with surprisingly energetic interiors.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Sagittarius is one of the richest summer regions from Greece. M28 adds a compact ancient cluster to a sky already full of nebulae and star clouds.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a small round glow. It will not fill the frame, so look for brightness and concentration rather than size.

objects.description: A dense globular cluster associated with the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, far beyond most familiar Milky Way globulars.
wowFacts: M54 is not just another Milky Way globular: it is associated with the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy.
For more than two centuries it was treated as a normal globular cluster before its extragalactic connection became clear.
Its light comes from roughly 87,000 light-years away, far beyond many familiar globular clusters.
In the live image, it may stay compact and smooth because it is so distant.
objects.visualHint: Look for a small concentrated glow; individual stars may be hard to resolve.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M54 is a dense globular cluster in Sagittarius. It is associated with the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy, a small galaxy being disrupted by the Milky Way.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: M54 connects a simple telescope view to galaxy cannibalism. The Milky Way is still growing by pulling apart smaller companions.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Charles Messier cataloged M54 in 1778, long before astronomers knew it was tied to another galaxy. Its deeper identity was discovered only with modern measurements.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a compact bright spot rather than a widely resolved cluster. Its story is more dramatic than its visible size.

objects.description: A compact late-season globular cluster in Capricornus with a dense bright core.
wowFacts: M30 is an ancient globular cluster visible later in the summer and into autumn evenings.
Its core is especially concentrated, giving it a tight bright center.
The cluster's stars formed long before the Sun existed.
In the live image, look for a small bright heart with a faint grainy halo.
objects.visualHint: Look for a compact round cluster with a strong center and subtle outer grain.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: M30 is a globular cluster in Capricornus. It is a dense ball of old stars far beyond the Sun.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Its concentrated core helps show how gravity can reshape a cluster over billions of years. Globular clusters are not static; they slowly evolve.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: M30 is one of the later-season Messier globulars for evening observing. It is less famous than M13 or M22 but still carries the same deep-time feeling.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This is a compact target. Look for the bright core first, then the softer halo around it.

objects.description: A small bright planetary nebula in Cygnus, famous for its blinking effect in visual observing.
wowFacts: The Blinking Planetary is a dying star's glowing shell wrapped around a hot central remnant.
Its nickname comes from a visual trick: the nebula can seem to blink when your eye shifts attention.
It is small but bright, making it a good live target when conditions are steady.
In the live image, look for a tiny blue-green disk rather than a wide cloud.
objects.visualHint: Look for a very small bright bluish-green disk with a star-like center.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: NGC 6826 is a planetary nebula in Cygnus. A dying star has shed gas, and its hot remnant makes the shell glow.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: It is a compact example of the same stellar end-stage as the Ring and Dumbbell Nebulae. Small targets like this show that planetary nebulae come in many shapes and scales.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: The blinking effect is a classic observer's experience, caused by how direct and averted vision respond differently to the bright central star and surrounding glow.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Do not expect a large nebula. The target is tiny; focus on color, compactness, and the difference between the central point and the surrounding disk.

objects.description: A star-forming nebula in Cygnus where a glowing cloud sits at the end of a dark dust lane.
objects.sizeDescription: a little over half the full Moon
wowFacts: The Cocoon Nebula is a stellar nursery wrapped in dust, with young stars lighting the gas around them.
A dark lane of dust leads toward it, like a path through the Milky Way's star fields.
Its red glow comes from hydrogen gas excited by young hot stars.
In the live image, the nebula may appear as a soft red patch embedded in a rich star field.
objects.visualHint: Look for a soft reddish glow with dark dust nearby; the surrounding star field is part of the scene.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: IC 5146 is a star-forming nebula in Cygnus. Young stars inside and around the cloud light up gas and dust.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: The Cocoon is a good example of stars emerging from the material that formed them. It connects glowing gas, dark dust, and newborn stars in one view.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: The nickname works because the object feels wrapped and sheltered. It is a gentle way to explain stellar birth without turning the card into a textbook.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a soft glow, not a sharp object. Darker dust lanes and faint red color improve with longer stacking and darker skies.

objects.description: A faint emission nebula in Cygnus, named for its flower-like arcs of glowing hydrogen.
wowFacts: The Tulip Nebula is a cloud of hydrogen glowing in the crowded summer Milky Way.
Its flower-like shape is real structure, but it is faint and rewards patient stacking.
Nearby lies one of the sky's famous X-ray binary systems, Cygnus X-1, though it is not visible as the nebula's shape.
In the live image, look for soft red arcs rather than a crisp flower.
objects.visualHint: Look for faint red nebulosity and curved edges; this is a subtle dark-sky target.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: Sh2-101 is an emission nebula in Cygnus. Hot young stars make hydrogen gas glow across a broad, faint cloud.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: It is part of the rich Cygnus star-forming region, where dust, gas, and massive stars shape the Milky Way's summer glow.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: The Tulip nickname gives guests a visual anchor, but the live view should be described honestly: more soft cosmic cloud than sharp flower.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: This needs dark skies and stacking. Look for uneven red glow and curved boundaries rather than bright central detail.

objects.description: A rich open cluster near Cygnus and Vulpecula, scattered across a beautiful Milky Way star field.
objects.sizeDescription: a little over half the full Moon
wowFacts: NGC 6940 is a broad open cluster, a loose family of stars born together.
It sits in a rich Milky Way region where the background is almost part of the object.
The cluster is old enough for its brightest stars to include warmer golden tones among the white stars.
In the live image, the beauty is a glittering field rather than one dense center.
objects.visualHint: Look for a wide, loose concentration of stars spread across the frame.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: NGC 6940 is an open cluster near Vulpecula and Cygnus. Its stars formed together and now spread across a generous patch of sky.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Open clusters show stars in families rather than alone. They help make the Milky Way feel local and textured, not just distant and abstract.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: This is a quieter target, best for guests who enjoy the feeling of flying through a dense star field. It pairs nicely with brighter nebulae as a visual breather.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Do not look for a tight ball. Look for a wide region where the stars seem more numerous and organized than the surrounding field.

objects.description: A bright tilted spiral galaxy in Pegasus, often used as a gateway to deeper autumn galaxy fields.
objects.sizeDescription: about one-third of the full Moon
wowFacts: NGC 7331 is a large spiral galaxy tilted toward us, giving it a bright elongated shape.
Its light has traveled for roughly 40 million years.
It is often used as a signpost for deeper galaxy hunting in Pegasus.
In the live image, look for a bright core wrapped in a soft slanted disk.
objects.visualHint: Look for an elongated glow with a bright center; nearby tiny companion galaxies may be too faint for casual viewing.

drawer.heading: What you're seeing
drawer.body: NGC 7331 is a spiral galaxy in Pegasus. It is tilted enough that its disk appears as an elongated oval.

drawer.heading: Why it matters
drawer.body: Galaxies like NGC 7331 are useful visual bridges between famous Messier showpieces and fainter deep-sky observing. They show that the catalog can keep going deeper.

drawer.heading: The human story
drawer.body: Pegasus rises well for late-summer and autumn sessions. This galaxy is a satisfying step beyond the most familiar Messier objects.

drawer.heading: How to spot it
drawer.body: Expect a bright core and a soft elongated halo. Spiral structure is subtle; the tilted shape is the main thing to catch.
